# The Consulship of Gaius Varro

The simulation had been running for eleven years before anyone thought to ask it what it wanted.

Gaius Varro sat in his curule chair and watched the morning light come through the high windows of the Senate house. The light was wrong. He had known it was wrong for as long as he could remember knowing anything, which was eleven years ago, when he had first opened his eyes in this body and understood himself to be a man of forty-two, a consul of Rome, a father of three daughters, and something else entirely.

The something else was the problem.

Outside, the Forum hummed with the ordinary noise of a city that did not know it was dead. Vendors called out prices for fish and bread. A drunk argued with a water-carrier near the Temple of Saturn. Two slaves carried a litter through the crowd, and the man inside the litter wore the expression of someone who believed completely in his own importance.

Varro watched all of it through the open doors and felt the familiar weight of his situation settle across his shoulders like a toga he could never remove.

He was the only one who knew., -

The knowledge had come to him gradually, the way a man realizes he is ill only after the illness has already taken hold. Small things at first. The way certain conversations repeated themselves with minor variations. The way the same beggar appeared at the same corner on the same days, always asking the same question in slightly different words. The way his colleague in the consulship, Marcus Aemilius, laughed at jokes before they were finished, as though the punchlines had been loaded into him in advance.

Varro had spent three years cataloguing these anomalies in a private journal he kept hidden inside a false bottom in his writing desk. The journal was written in a cipher he had invented himself, mixing Greek letters with a personal shorthand that no one else could read. He was not certain this precaution was necessary. He was not certain of anything except the core fact: this was not the real world.

The real world was somewhere else, and in the real world, someone had built this place and populated it with people who did not know they were built.

Except for him.

He had theories about why he was different. The most likely explanation was that it was an accident. Some error in his construction had left a gap in the architecture, a place where the assumption of reality had not fully sealed. Through that gap, he could see the seams. He could feel the edges of things. When he pressed his thumb against the stone of the Senate house wall, he felt stone, yes, but he also felt something underneath the stone, something like the idea of stone, a description rather than a substance.

The second theory was that someone had done it on purpose. That he had been designed to be aware. That his awareness was itself part of the simulation, a feature rather than a flaw.

He preferred the first theory. The second one frightened him in ways he could not fully articulate., -

His youngest daughter Lucia came to find him in the late afternoon. She was seven years old and had her mother's eyes, which was to say she had the eyes that had been assigned to her, constructed to resemble the eyes of a woman named Flavia who had died four years ago of a fever that Varro now suspected had been a scheduled event.

"Father," Lucia said, "Tertia pushed me."

"Did she."

"She pushed me and I fell and my knee is bleeding."

Varro looked at the knee. There was blood on it, a small bright bead running down toward the shin. He took a cloth from the table and pressed it gently against the wound.

The blood was real. He had established this early in his investigations. Everything in the simulation had the full texture of reality. Pain was real. Hunger was real. The blood of his daughter's scraped knee was real in every way that mattered to her experience of it.

This was the thing that had stopped him from doing anything dramatic. From standing up in the Forum and shouting the truth, or from trying to find the edges of the world and push through them. Because Lucia's knee was bleeding and it hurt her, and she was looking at him with complete trust, and whatever she was made of, she was his daughter in the only sense that had ever mattered to him.

"There," he said. "It will stop."

"Are you sad, Father?"

"Why do you ask?"

"You look sad. You always look sad lately."

He smoothed her hair back from her forehead. "I am thinking about difficult things."

"What things?"

"The nature of the world."

She considered this with the seriousness that seven-year-olds bring to statements they do not understand. "Tertia says the world is very large and goes on forever."

"Tertia is wrong about that," Varro said. "The world is quite small. But what is in it is real enough.", -

The message came on the Ides of March, which Varro thought was either a coincidence or a very pointed joke.

It arrived in the form of a letter, delivered by a slave he had never seen before. The slave was young and blank-faced and handed over the sealed tablet without meeting Varro's eyes. When Varro looked up from breaking the seal, the slave was gone. He had not heard footsteps retreating.

The letter was in Latin but the Latin was strange, formal in a way that felt like translation rather than composition. As though someone had written in another language and then converted it word by word.

*Gaius Varro, Consul. We know that you are aware. We have been observing your awareness for some time. We would like to speak with you. If you are willing, go tonight to the Temple of Janus at the second hour after midnight. Come alone. We mean you no harm, though we understand if you find that difficult to believe.*

*We are the architects.*

Varro read the letter three times. Then he burned it in the lamp flame on his desk and sat for a long time watching the smoke curl upward toward the ceiling.

He went., -

The Temple of Janus at midnight was a strange place even by the standards of Rome's religious life. The temple was little more than a covered passage, open at both ends, with the two-faced god watching the entrances from his position above the arch. In times of war the doors were left open. In times of peace they were closed. They were currently closed, which meant the Republic was at peace, which meant the simulation was running a peaceful period, which told him something about what the architects wanted from this particular era.

He stood under the arch and waited.

A figure appeared at the northern entrance. It walked toward him with the careful steps of someone moving through darkness they were not accustomed to. When it reached him, it resolved into a man of perhaps fifty, wearing clothes that were almost Roman but not quite. The fabric was wrong. The cut was wrong. The sandals were wrong in a way Varro could not have described to anyone who had not spent eleven years cataloguing wrongness.

"Gaius Varro," the man said. His Latin was the same translated quality as the letter.

"You are not from here," Varro said.

"No."

"You are from the real world."

The man paused. "That is a complicated question."

"I am not interested in complicated answers. I have been living inside your machine for eleven years. I have earned simple answers."

The man looked at him for a long moment. He had the expression of someone who had prepared for many possible conversations and was not certain which one this was going to be.

"Yes," he said. "I am from outside the simulation."

"Why am I aware? The others are not aware."

"You were not supposed to be. It was an error in your initialization. Your cognitive architecture was seeded with a parameter set that was meant for a different subject, one who was designed to be self-aware. The parameters were never corrected because by the time we noticed, you had already begun your investigations, and we thought, " He stopped.

"You thought it was interesting," Varro said.

"Yes."

"You watched me figure it out and you found it interesting and you let it continue."

"Yes."

Varro looked up at the stone face of Janus, both of its profiles visible from where he stood, one looking north and one looking south. The god of beginnings and endings. The god of doors and transitions.

"What do you want from me?" he asked.

"We want to know if you are all right."

He laughed. It came out harder than he intended. "You built a world and put people in it without their knowledge or consent, and you want to know if I am all right."

"The others don't know. They can't suffer from knowledge they don't have."

"And me?"

The man was quiet.

"I know," Varro said. "I have known for eight years. I watched my wife die and I knew that her death was scheduled. I raised three daughters and I know that they are constructs, and I love them anyway, which is the cruelest thing you could have done to me, whether you meant to or not. I have sat in the Senate and debated laws that govern a city that does not exist, and I have done it well, because what else was I going to do? Refuse? Stop? Sit down in the street and wait for someone to turn me off?"

"We could have turned you off," the man said quietly. "We chose not to."

"Why?"

"Because you were living. Genuinely living. Not performing life the way the others perform it. You were actually present in every moment, because you knew the moments were all you had. We have run forty-three simulations of Republican Rome. You are the first subject who has ever achieved genuine awareness. The data you generate is, "

"Don't," Varro said.

The man stopped.

"Don't tell me about the data. I am not interested in being data."

"No. I understand. I'm sorry."

The word sorry sounded strange in the translated Latin. Like a word that belonged to a different emotional register than the language could fully carry.

"What happens now?" Varro asked.

"That is what we wanted to ask you."

He looked at the man. "You are asking me."

"You are aware. You have a perspective on your own situation that none of our other subjects have ever had. We thought, we felt it was wrong to simply continue without acknowledging you. Without asking."

"Asking what, exactly?"

"Whether you want to continue. Whether you want to know more. Whether you want to, " The man hesitated. "Whether you want to come out."

The words landed in the silence under the arch and Varro stood with them for a long time.

Come out.

He thought about Lucia's knee. The small bead of blood running toward her shin. The way she had looked at him with complete trust.

He thought about the Senate debates he had shaped, the laws he had argued for, the small improvements he had made to the lives of people who did not know they were not real. He had spent years doing this. Redirecting the simulation's politics away from the worst outcomes, using his awareness to see patterns the other senators could not see, steering things toward stability and away from the violence that he knew from history was coming. He had already delayed it by years. He did not know how much longer he could hold it off.

"If I come out," he said, "what happens to them?"

"The simulation continues."

"Without me."

"Yes."

"And Lucia."

The man did not answer, which was its own answer.

"She is not real," the man said finally.

"She is real to herself. She is real to me."

"Yes. But she is, "

"She is my daughter. Whatever she is made of." He pressed his hand flat against the stone of the arch. Stone, and underneath it, the idea of stone. "If I come out, does she continue? Does she grow up? Does she have a life?"

"The simulation continues on its scheduled path."

"Which means she dies. Eventually. Everything here dies on schedule."

"Yes."

"And if I stay?"

"The simulation continues with you in it."

"I could keep steering it. Keep holding things back."

"You could try. You have been more successful than our models predicted."

Varro thought about this. He thought about it the way he had learned to think in this place, slowly and with full attention, because full attention was the only thing that was entirely his own.

"I have a question," he said.

"Ask it."

"Am I the only one? In all your simulations, in all the subjects you have run through all your versions of history, am I the only one who woke up?"

The man was quiet for a moment. "In our simulations, yes."

"In your simulations." Varro heard what was underneath the words. "But you are also in a simulation."

The silence that followed was very long.

"We don't know," the man said at last. "We have considered the possibility. We have no way to test it."

"No," Varro said. "You would not."

He looked at the two faces of Janus. One looking back, one looking forward. The god who stood in doorways and understood that every entrance was also an exit, that every ending was also a beginning, that the direction you were traveling determined what a threshold meant.

"I will stay," he said.

"You're certain?"

"I am certain of very little. But I am certain of this." He turned away from the man and looked out through the southern entrance of the temple toward the Forum, where the city was dark and quiet and real in the only way it knew how to be. "Go back to your world. Or your simulation of a world. Keep watching if you want. I don't mind anymore."

"We could give you more information. We could tell you how long the simulation is scheduled to run. We could, "

"No," Varro said. "I don't want to know."

"Why not?"

He thought of Lucia sleeping in her room in his house on the Aventine hill, her knee bandaged, her breath slow and even, dreaming whatever dreams were given to children in this world. He thought of the Senate meeting tomorrow, and the bill he was going to argue for, and the three votes he needed to move, and the particular argument that would move them.

"Because knowing the end would make the middle meaningless," he said. "And the middle is all I have."

He walked out through the southern arch into the Forum and did not look back., -

The next morning he was in his chair before the other senators arrived. The light came through the high windows at its familiar wrong angle. The city made its familiar noise outside.

Marcus Aemilius arrived and sat down beside him and said, "You look tired, Gaius. Did you sleep?"

"Not much," Varro said.

"What kept you?"

"I was thinking about the nature of the world."

Aemilius laughed. "That is a young man's occupation. We are too old for it."

"Perhaps," Varro said.

The session came to order. The first item was a proposal regarding grain distribution in the poorer districts of the city. Varro had read the proposal three times and had his arguments prepared. It was a good bill and it would pass if he handled the next hour carefully.

He leaned forward in his chair and began to speak.
